work.title: Stoic at Work
work.subtitle: 7 days to a calmer view of work

work.title: Why do you get up?
work.read:
The alarm goes off for the third time. You hit snooze and, under the duvet, run through the day’s list: meetings, emails, a file that never ends. You can’t find a single reason to get up.

The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius didn’t want to get out of bed some mornings either. In a note to himself he admits it and asks: I’m getting up to do the work of a human being; if that’s what I was born for, why am I complaining? Was I made to lie under the warm blankets?

People look for the meaning of work in a big title or a salary. Yet most of the time it sits somewhere much smaller: in the life of a single person your work touches. Someone who gets an invoice right, greets a patient with a smile, writes code with care makes someone’s day easier.

The baker takes the bread out before sunrise; the person reaching for warm bread at that hour never meets them, but has been touched by them.

What you’re getting up for today has a face. Seeing it makes the alarm a little lighter.
work.body: Write in one sentence who your work is for: a particular person, a face. When the day gets hard, come back to that sentence.
work.ask: Did your work touch someone today? What did you feel when you noticed it?

work.title: One task
work.read:
You’re writing a report; halfway through, a message comes in. While you look at it, an email comes to mind; when you open the email, you see the meeting on your calendar. The day ends, and no task does.

Marcus writes to himself: do the task in front of you as if it were the last of your life, free of distraction, hurry and pretense. War, court cases and letters were waiting on his desk all at once; still, he urges himself back to the one task in front of him.

People think getting a lot done means doing many things at once. It doesn’t. The more your attention splits, the longer each task takes and the more it tires you. Most of the tiredness comes not from the work itself, but from jumping endlessly from one task to the next.

With the single candle in your hand you light one corner of the room; try to stretch it across the whole room and you can’t see anything.

The quiet relief of one finished task is worth more than the noise of ten half-done ones.
work.body: Do one task with notifications off, without opening another tab, until it’s done.
work.ask: How did time pass when you stayed with one task? What felt different?

work.title: Do less
work.read:
Your calendar is full, your to-do list is long. Looking back in the evening, you can’t tell how much of it was really necessary; you’re just tired.

Marcus passes on advice from an old philosopher: if you want peace, do little. Then he corrects it: or rather, do what is necessary. Most of what we say and do isn’t necessary; let it go, and you’re left with both time and calm.

This isn’t laziness. Doing less isn’t running away, it’s choosing. Whoever says “yes” to everything has really said “no” to what matters. Letting go of the unnecessary makes room for the necessary.

The gardener prunes even the beautiful branches; the tree gives its fruit to the ones that remain.

Let go of one thing today. The lightness will come not from the work you do, but from the work you don’t.
work.body: Drop one unnecessary task, meeting or message. Three times during the day, ask: “Is this necessary?”
work.ask: What did you let go of today? What happened when you did?

work.title: The difficult colleague
work.read:
There’s someone who interrupts you in meetings, dumps their work on you and takes little jabs at you in emails. Even seeing their name on the screen makes your shoulders tense.

Every morning Marcus reminded himself: today I’ll meet rude, ungrateful, envious people. But they’re human like me; they act this way because they can’t tell good from bad. We were made to work together, like hands, feet and teeth.

This doesn’t mean putting up with everything. You can set boundaries, speak plainly, and complain if you need to. The Stoic simply separates the other person’s behavior from their own: their rudeness is theirs, your response is yours.

If a rower gets angry because the person beside them lost the rhythm, and drops their own oar too, the boat never moves forward.

You may not be able to change them. But you don’t have to hand your day over to them.
work.body: Take one step toward working together with a colleague you find difficult. In the evening, write their behavior and your response on two separate lines.
work.ask: Today, could you find a space between their behavior and your response?

work.title: Unpraised work
work.read:
Someone else presented the work you’d spent weeks on, and no one mentioned your name. Or a job you’ve done well for years only got noticed the day it slipped.

Marcus asks himself: does something get better because it’s praised? Is an emerald any less an emerald because no one praises it? Gold, a flower, a knife; they’re all what they are, even if no one looks.

Wanting recognition is nothing to be ashamed of. But if you tie the worth of your work to someone else’s eyes, every time those eyes close, you go out too. Work done well is good even if no one sees it; and the one who did it knows that.

The stone mason carves the statue at the top of the cathedral, where no one will ever see it, with the same care.

Being seen is lovely. But it isn’t necessary for being good.
work.body: Do a piece of work no one will see, with care, and tell no one.
work.ask: How did it feel to do something well with no one watching?

work.title: The mistake
work.read:
You sent the wrong file, missed a deadline, gave a client the wrong number. In that moment, a knot in your stomach; even lying in bed at night, it keeps turning over in your mind.

Marcus writes to himself: when you fail to act by your principles, don’t be disgusted, don’t lose hope, don’t give up. When you fall, come back; and if most of what you do is worthy of a human being, be content.

Ignoring a mistake and punishing yourself with it lead to the same place: learning nothing from it. The weight of a mistake usually comes not from its consequences, but from the verdict you pass on yourself: “I’m useless.” Yet a mistake is an event, not an identity.

The traveler who stumbles on the road stops, ties their shoe and keeps walking; they don’t walk the whole road again from the start.

Accepting a mistake means you don’t have to carry it.
work.body: After a mistake, ask three questions: What happened? What was my part? What will I do next time? Write down the answers, then let it go.
work.ask: How did you look at a mistake today? What changed when you asked questions instead of passing a verdict?

work.title: Rest
work.read:
You got home in the evening, but your mind is still at work. Even on weekends you check your emails. Rest feels like a luxury, even a crime.

Seneca writes that the mind can’t stay tense all the time: even the most fertile field turns barren if it’s never left to rest. Socrates wasn’t ashamed to play with children; Cato eased the day’s burden in the evening with a glass of wine. A mind that relaxes rises stronger.

Rest isn’t laziness; it’s part of the work. Whoever knows how to stop as well as how to work can walk the long road. Whoever never stops will one day be forced to.

A bow that is always drawn loses its strength; when the archer isn’t using it, they loosen the string.

Today you’re allowed to stop. And if the tiredness hasn’t lifted for months, if your sleep and appetite are off, talking to a professional is a Stoic choice too.
work.body: Plan a real break, without screens, and protect it like a meeting.
work.ask: Did you really rest today? How has the way you see work changed over these seven days?
